planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions 1-2 inches deep in spring after the last frost into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; commercially sold stock is generally less hardy than high-elevation wild forms, so mulch well at the cold end of its range.

directions: Plant divisions of the slender pseudobulbs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade. Arching, grass-like leaves are topped in late spring to early summer by loose spikes of 3-7 nodding, cattleya-like flowers in pale pink to white, each lip marked with deep yellow and red spots. Native from Taiwan and Japan's Ryukyu Islands through several Chinese provinces at elevations from about 2,000 to 9,500 feet, giving the species a wide range of cold tolerance depending on provenance; most plants in commerce are hardy to roughly zone 7, while higher-elevation collections may tolerate more cold. Divide congested clumps in early spring and mulch over winter at the cooler end of its range.

planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions 1-2 inches deep in spring into fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade; mulch heavily in zone 5-6 gardens, where this cultivar needs winter protection.

directions: A named selection of the Chinese ground orchid grown for flower color: lavender blooms with a distinct blue cast, a darker lavender-purple lip edge flecked with spotting, and a honey-yellow throat, carried on 14-18 inch stems above pleated, strap-shaped foliage in spring and summer. The cultivar name honors Murasaki Shikibu, the Heian-era Japanese author of The Tale of Genji, a common naming convention among Japanese-bred ornamental selections. Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade; it is hardy in zone 6-9, with protection needed in zone 5. Divide congested clumps in early spring before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, well-drained, humus-rich woodland soil in a sheltered, partly shaded to shaded site; considered among the hardiest Calanthe species, tolerating brief cold to about 14F with protection in harsher winters.

directions: Plant divisions into moist, well-drained, humus-rich woodland soil in a sheltered site in shade to part shade. Evergreen to semi-evergreen ribbed leaves form a clump 12-18 inches tall and wide, topped in late winter to early spring by erect racemes of nodding, yellow-green flowers with a ruffled, reddish-brown lip. Native from northern Pakistan across temperate Asia to Japan, it is regarded as one of the hardiest species in the genus, tolerating brief temperatures down to about 14F, though foliage may go deciduous in prolonged hard freezes. Naturalizes modestly by offsets into an expanding woodland clump; avoid disturbing established plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered partly shaded site that stays consistently damp; in the wild it grows along stream edges and seepage slopes, so it tolerates and benefits from more moisture than most terrestrial orchids.

directions: Plant divisions into evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, partly shaded site. Clumps of long, pleated, evergreen leaves send up unbranched flower spikes bearing up to 25 scented blooms, pale lilac petals surrounding an elongated purple-violet lip, opening in succession from late July into September, unusually late for a hardy orchid, flowering through the hottest part of summer. Native to Japan from Kyushu to Hokkaido, where its Japanese name natsuebine ('summer shrimp root') reflects both its summer bloom time and habitat in wet woodlands, mountain streamsides, and seepage areas that commonly flood. Tolerates brief cold to about 14F. Keep soil consistently damp rather than merely moist.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into average to slightly moist, fertile, well-drained soil in part sun; one of the more cold-hardy Spiranthes species, suited to zone 4-9 gardens.

directions: Plant divisions into average to slightly moist, fertile, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade. A small rosette of glossy, pointed leaves with velvety roots sends up a tightly packed, spiraled flower spike to about 15 inches in late summer, bearing tiny lavender-pink flowers with a white lip winding around the stem. Native to China, Japan, and Korea, where it grows in grassy meadows, and hardy from zone 4 to 9b, a notably wider cold range than many terrestrial orchids. Regularly produces new shoots under good conditions; avoid letting soil dry out for extended periods during active growth.

planting.note: Plant only laboratory-propagated, nursery-grown rhizomes, set shallowly into moist, well-drained, organic-rich soil in part to full shade; seed-grown plants typically take 6-8 years to reach flowering size, so purchase flowering-size nursery stock rather than seedlings if bloom is wanted soon.

directions: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-culture or seed-grown rhizomes (never wild-collected) shallowly into moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, in part to full shade. A widespread but highly variable species across China, Russia, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, it bears large, dramatic flowers in deep glowing magenta-pink with a huge rounded pouch and broad striped petals in May. It is the species parent (with C. flavum) behind the easier garden hybrid Cypripedium 'Gisela.' Like all Cypripedium, it is CITES Appendix II listed and subject to collection pressure in parts of its wild range, so source stock only from reputable propagators; seed-grown plants take roughly 6-8 years to reach flowering size. Site in a cool, humus-rich woodland bed and avoid disturbing established clumps.
